Internally BN-Doped Coronene
Jing-Cai Zeng, Xuan-Yu Song, Ze-Fan Yao, Yong-Shi Chen, Yu-Chun Xu, Kexiang Zhao,
Yi Liu, Jie-Yu Wang,* and Jian Pei*
Abstract: We present the ﬁrst synthesis of internally
BN-doped coronenes (B2N2-C, H-B2N2-C, and 2H-
B2N2-C) with two covalent B─N units embedded on
the central axis of coronene. The B─N doping leads
to unique electronic structures with distinct charge
distribution, conjugation, aromaticity, and photophysical
properties. The structures were successfully identiﬁed
by the single-crystal X-ray scattering. B2N2-C without
sidechains retains the structure of coronene but exhibits
stronger π–π stacking, higher electronic coupling, and
a narrowed solid-state bandgap. Driven by the B─N
dipole–dipole interaction, all B2N2-coronene derivatives
exhibit more ordered assembly with excimer emission in
solution, which is absent in coronene. Notably, two stable
polymorphs emerge in single crystals of 2H-B2N2-C with
two hexyl chains: a kinetically stable rod phase and a
thermodynamically stable plate phase, where variations
in processing conditions direct the formation of different
phases.
Introduction
Coronene, a D6h symmetric perifused PAH ﬁrst isolated in
1932 by Scholl and Meyer,[1] represents the smallest analogue
of benzene with sixfold symmetry among many benzenoid
PAHs.[2] The perfect delocalization of aromaticity across the
six outer rings endows it with a unique electronic structure.[3,4]
In the crystalline state, the large overlap of neighboring π
planes with compact packing facilitates the easy transport of
charge carriers.[5] Coronene has been the important structural
motif of 2D nanostructures such as nanographenes,[6–9]
graphene
quantum
dots,[10]
and
conductive
frame
materials.[11–13] These unique 2D structures hold critical
applications in materials science and biomedical science,[14]

such as charge transport,[15–21] supramolecular assembly,[22–24]
optical waveguide,[25] phosphorescent emission,[26] circularly
polarized light (CPL) emission,[27] bioprobing,[28] and drug
delivery.[29] To expand the properties and applications of
coronene, extensive research has been dedicated to the
structure modiﬁcations of coronene, such as the conjugation
extension and incorporation of heteroatoms such as N, S,
P, and B atoms.[30–32] The incorporation of heteroatoms
proves to fundamentally alter the electronic structures and
supramolecular assembly, offering opportunities for tailoring
optoelectronic properties. In 1982, Tokita et al. reported the
ﬁrst N-substituted coronenes (1,2-diazacoronene and 1,2,7,8-
tetraazacoronene).[33, 34] Later, derivatives of 1,5,9-triaza-
coronene,[35,36] 1,7-diazacoronene,[37] 1,8-diazacoronene,[37]
1,2,5,6,9-pentaazacoronene,[38]
and
1,4,7,10-tetraazacoro-
nene[39] were synthesized by Wei, Cheng, Xiao, and Gade
et al. The N-doping endows the molecules with low-lying
frontier orbital energy levels and enhanced ﬂuorescence
quantum yields, making coronene a potential emissive
material and n-type organic semiconductor.
Among various heteroatoms, embedding PAHs with B─N
units has stood out as a novel and effective approach over
the past few years.[40–42] As the isoelectronic unit of the C═C
bond, the covalent B─N bond could alter the distribution
of molecular orbitals and deepen the energy levels, which
also stabilizes the conjugated skeleton toward oxidation.[43,44]
Signiﬁcantly, the dipolar nature of B─N units provides
additional intermolecular interactions, which could be uti-
lized to construct unique supramolecular architectures.[45]
Developed by Dewar, Ashe, Liu, Piers, Vaquero, and Wagner
et al.,[40,41] classic BN-PAHs, such as BN-naphthalene,[46,47]
BN-anthracene,[43,48] BN-phenanthrene,[49–52] BN-pyrene,[53]
and BN-perylene,[45,54–56] have been reported. To date, four
peripheral B─N embedded coronene derivatives have been
synthesized by several research groups (Figure 1a).[32,57–61]
It was found that B─N doping of coronene altered the
energy levels and improved the quantum yields. However,
in all the reported structures, the heteroatoms including the
B─N unit were incorporated at the periphery of coronene
(Figure S1), and the internally heteroatom-doped coronenes
remained elusive, possibly due to limitations in molecular
design strategies and synthetic methods. The unexplored
internally heteroatom-doped coronene and the fascinating
advantages endowed by B─N units urge us to seek the
internally BN-doped coronenes.
Herein, we present the ﬁrst synthesis of internally BN-
doped coronenes (B2N2-C, H-B2N2-C, and 2H-B2N2-C,
where H means n-hexyl) (Figure 1b). The electronic structure
and photophysical properties of coronene change signiﬁcantly

ysis shows that B2N2-C adopts a similar arrangement to
coronene, but exhibits enhanced π–π stacking, boosted
electronic coupling, and a reduced solid bandgap compared
to coronene. The dipolar nature of B─N promotes the orderly
assembly and enables excimer emissions for all three B2N2-

Results and Discussion
The synthetic route of the B2N2-coronenes is shown in
Scheme 1. Suzuki–Miyaura coupling of 1 with different
boron reagents produced 2 (66%) and 9 (85%). The
unsymmetric derivative 6 was synthesized through two-step
Suzuki–Miyaura couplings via 5. Notably, only 2 was reduced
quantitatively with sodium dithionite in the classical mixed
protonic solvent EtOH/H2O system,[56] whereas 6 and 9
with more hydrophobic alkyl chains required the more
hydrophobic i-PrOH/H2O system. The reduction products
3, 7, and 10 reacted with potassium ethynyltriﬂuoroborate
through electrophilic borylation to give the B2N2-perylene
derivatives 4 (57%), 8 (42%), and 11 (74%). Single-crystal
X-ray diffraction (SCXRD) of 4 suggested that the distance
between the alkyne cyclization reaction sites is 3.607–
3.651 Å, exceeding the distance of 3.4 Å summarized in the
literature.[62] Therefore, the subsequent alkyne cyclization
catalyzed by PtCl2 needs to be carried out at an elevated tem-
perature of 145 °C. Finally, B2N2-C (32%), H-B2N2-C (18%),
and 2H-B2N2-C (23%) were obtained in moderate yields.
InCl3 was also employed, but the yield was 10% for B2N2-
C. B2N2-C has poor solubility in common solvents, such as
dichloromethane, toluene, and ethyl acetate, which was ﬁnally
puriﬁed by vacuum sublimation at 250 °C and 10−6 mbar.
H-B2N2-C and 2H-B2N2-C showed better solubility and
were puriﬁed by preparative gel permeation chromatography
(GPC). The chemical structures of these B2N2-coronenes
were identiﬁed by combined characterizations of nuclear
magnetic resonance (NMR) spectroscopy, high-resolution
mass spectrometry (HRMS), infrared (IR) spectroscopy, and
SCXRD. The decomposition temperatures at 5% weight loss
were recorded for coronene (341 °C), B2N2-C (331 °C),
H-B2N2-C (352 °C), and 2H-B2N2-C (326 °C), respectively
(Figure S6a), indicating their good thermal stability. Notably,
B2N2-coronenes exhibited good stabilities under ambient
conditions and remained intact even after prolonged storage
of several months, in stark contrast to coronene, which gradu-
ally decomposed under the same conditions. This suggests that
the B─N doping can improve the ambient stability of large
conjugated PAHs.[44]
The electronic structures of B2N2-C and coronene were
further investigated (Figure 1b). B2N2-C exhibits a polar-
ized and more positive electrostatic potential (ESP) than
coronene. The localized orbital locator of π orbitals (LOL-π)
indicates that the periphery of coronene exhibits characteris-
tics of the double bond.[63] B2N2-C shows partial conjugation
on the B─N bond and adopts conjugation features of the
divinylbenzene. The aromaticity was further investigated by
anisotropy of the induced current density (ACID) plot and
nucleus-independent chemical shifts (NICS).[4,64,65] Coronene
exhibits a clockwise ring current in the periphery, suggesting
global aromaticity. The introduction of B─N disrupts the
global aromaticity with the central N2C4 ring exhibiting
obvious antiaromaticity (NICS(1)ZZ = 24.2) (Figure 1b).
Due to the same conjugated skeleton, B2N2-coronenes
exhibit
similar
absorptions
and
ﬂuorescence
emissions
(Figure 2). The optical gap of B2N2-C was measured
to be 3.11 eV, which is larger than that of coronene
(2.86 eV). The maximum emission wavelength of B2N2-C
(425 nm) is also blueshifted compared to that of coronene
(446 nm) (Figure 2b). Three B2N2-coronenes all have less
well-resolved ﬁne structures, implying weakened molecular
rigidity. According to the calculation results, the weak lowest-
energy absorption bands of coronene and B2N2-coronenes
are attributed to the S0→S1 transition. It is worth noting that
B2N2-coronenes exhibit strong absorptions around 280 nm,
which match the electronic transition of divinylbenzene,
indicating the partial conjugation in B2N2-coronenes. The
photoluminescence quantum yield of B2N2-C (PLQY = 0.28)
is higher than that of coronene (PLQY = 0.07). Besides,
the radiative transition rate of B2N2-C (kr = 7.5 × 107 s−1)
is also higher than that of coronene (kr = 2.6 × 106 s−1).

Considering the strong π stacking of coronene, the aggre-
gation behaviors of B2N2-coronenes in high-concentrated
solution were studied (Figure 3). With the increase in
concentration, the high-energy vibrational emission peaks of
B2N2-coronenes gradually weaken, whereas the low-energy
vibrational emission peaks gradually strengthen, showing the
H-aggregation characteristics.[66–68] When the concentration
reaches above 10−3 M, a new redshifted and broadened
emission peak emerges for each B2N2-coronene, which is
not observed for coronene. Subsequent ﬂuorescence lifetime
measurements show that each B2N2-coronene exhibits two
ﬂuorescence lifetimes at above 10−3 M (4.44 and 6.54 ns
for B2N2-C, 5.09 and 9.14 ns for H-B2N2-C, and 6.44 and
9.78 ns for 2H-B2N2-C) (Figure S30), corresponding to two
emissive species. The newly emerged redshifted emission
peak shows a longer lifetime, which agrees with the prolonged
lifetime of the excimer-like states.[69] This indicates that
B2N2-coronenes form more ordered aggregations in solution,
which could be attributed to the intermolecular B─N dipole–
dipole interaction. The maximum emission wavelengths of the

The cyclic voltammetry measurements show that coronene
and B2N2-coronenes all have irreversible redox behaviors
(Figure S33), implying the instabilities of corresponding
radical cations and anions. The frontier molecular orbital
(FMO) energy levels were obtained through theoretical
calculation (Figure S34). The HOMO level of B2N2-C
is −5.70 eV, similar to that of coronene (−5.72 eV). The
LUMO level of B2N2-C is slightly decreased from −1.63 eV
(coronene) to −1.77 eV. The doping of B─N slightly narrows
the HOMO–LUMO gap from 4.09 eV (coronene) to 3.93 eV.
It is noted that the trend in the HOMO–LUMO gap does
not align with the observed optical gap in the solution. This
discrepancy arises from the fact that, for coronene and B2N2-
C, the S0→S1 electronic transitions are not predominantly
governed by the HOMO→LUMO transitions, as indicated
by Tables S1 and S2.
Table 1 was summarized to further compare the prop-
erties of B2N2-C with coronene and with the peripherally
substituted BN-coronene (C) by Yu/Liu (2022) to highlight
the signiﬁcance of this new compound.[61] B2N2-C exhibits
a notably higher HOMO–LUMO gap, a lower PLQY, and
a shorter ﬂuorescence lifetime compared to compound C.
The kr of B2N2-C is also signiﬁcantly smaller than that of
compound C while exhibiting a notably higher knr. This can
be rationalized by the signiﬁcantly increased reorganization
energy of B2N2-C, signifying the profound effects of the B─N
position on the structure.
The crystal structures of coronene, B2N2-C, and 2H-
B2N2-C were successfully resolved to analyze their packing
structures in solid state.[71] Unfortunately, single crystals of
H-B2N2-C suitable for X-ray crystallography could not be
obtained with various trials of cultivation conditions. As
shown in Figure 4a, the length of double bonds in the
periphery of coronene is 1.361 Å, shorter than the delocalized
bond length of 1.391 Å in benzene and close to the C═C
double bond in ethylene (1.331 Å).[3,72] B2N2-C exhibits a
fully planar geometry similar to coronene (Figure 4b). The
length of B─N bond in B2N2-C is 1.443 Å, close to the
partially delocalized B─N bond length of 1.446 Å.[73] The
C═C bond length in the periphery is further shortened to
1.348 Å with an increased double-bond feature, indicating
the partial conjugation of B2N2-C. Unusually, B2N2-C
displays a similar herringbone arrangement with similar
dislocation, π–π overlap, and cell parameters compared with
coronene (Figure 4d,e). But the π–π stacking distance is
shortened from 3.42 to 3.39 Å, implying the enhanced π–
π stacking by the B─N dipole–dipole interactions. With
the addition of alkyl chains, 2H-B2N2-C shows two stable
polymorphs (Figure S35), 2H-B2N2-C-rod and 2H-B2N2-C-
plate (Figure 4c). In the rod phase, 2H-B2N2-C forms a
1D columnar packing (Figure 4f). The introduction of alkyl
chains increases the π–π stacking distance (3.39–3.41 Å)
and reduces the π–π overlap (43%–40%) slightly. A layered
arrangement is formed in the plate phase with a dominant
C─Hπ interaction (Figure 4g), showing a layer distance
of 3.55 Å without signiﬁcant π–π overlap (0%). Notably,
all the B─N dipoles of B2N2-coronenes are parallel in the
solid state, further demonstrating that the B─N dipole–dipole
interactions promote the ordered molecular assembly.
It is noted that the distinct crystal phases of 2H-B2N2-C
could be obtained by controlling the crystallization con-
ditions. The rod phase was yielded through programmed
recrystallization (20 °C h−1 ramping from 85 to 30 °C)
from a toluene solution. The plate phase was obtained by a
slower crystallization process such as the slow evaporation
of toluene solution or the diffusion of methanol vapor to

To further understand the packing behaviors and explore
the nature of B─N dipole–dipole interaction in crystals, the
noncovalent interaction (NCI) energies between molecules
were calculated (Figure S38), as quantitative studies on
the intermolecular interactions of BN-PAHs are scarce.
The interaction energies are calculated with the sobE-
DAw method.[74,75] The total interaction energy (Eint) is
decomposed as Eint = Eels + Exrep + Eorb + Edisp, where
Eels represents the electrostatic term, Exrep represents the
exchange-repulsion term, Eorb represents the orbital terms,
and Edisp represents the dispersion term. The calculation
results showed that Eint (π–π interaction energy) of coronene
is −17.12 kcal mol−1 with a lattice energy of −34.42 kcal
mol−1. B2N2-C exhibits a higher Eint of −18.39 kcal mol−1
and a higher lattice energy of −36.97 kcal mol−1. The B─N
dipole leads to an increment of −1.27 kcal mol−1 in interaction
energy, which is mainly increased by the electrostatic term
and dispersion term. This nature of the B─N dipole–dipole
interaction is similar to the weak H-bond (less than −2.5 kcal
mol−1) dominated by electrostatics and dispersion.[76,77]
With the addition of alkyl chains, the Eint of 2H-B2N2-
C-rod increases to −25.35 kcal mol−1, whereas the lattice
energy increases to −58.58 kcal mol−1. To determine the π–
π interaction energy, the π-conjugated skeleton (named π–π
(rod)) is abstracted from the 2H-B2N2-C-rod by removing
the alkyl chains. The Eint of π–π (rod) is weakened to
−16.50 kcal mol−1 compared to B2N2-C (−18.39 kcal mol−1),
which is attributed to the reduced π–π overlap and enlarged
π–π distance. The 2H-B2N2-C-plate shows a smaller Eint
(−23.02 kcal mol−1) than 2H-B2N2-C-rod but higher lattice
energy (65.30 kcal mol−1) with a more dense packing (cell
density: 2H-B2N2-C-plate (1.258 g cm−3) > 2H-B2N2-C-
rod (1.224 g cm−3)) (Figure S36), which explains the kinetic
formation of 2H-B2N2-C-rod and the thermodynamically
stable characteristic of 2H-B2N2-C-plate. The Eint of π–π
(plate) is very weak (−3.84 kcal mol−1) due to the zero π–π
overlap.

The similar
arrangement of
coronene and B2N2-C
inspired us to determine the inﬂuencing radius of B─N dipole
on molecular assembly, which has not been disclosed before.
After the survey and calculation of reported BN-PAHs
with different sizes (Figures S39–S41), the size-dependent
assembly convergence effect may exist in BN-PAHs: although
B─N dipoles cause distinct assembly in small PAHs, large BN-
PAHs are likely to adopt packing modes similar to parent
PAHs as intrinsic intermolecular interactions prevail.
The UV–vis–NIR diffuse reﬂection spectroscopy of pow-
ders was conducted to study the electronic structures of solids.
As shown in Figure 5a,b, the bandgaps of solids are in the
trend of coronene (2.53 eV) > 2H-B2N2-C (2.26 eV) > H-
B2N2-C (2.12 eV) and B2N2-C (2.12 eV). The maximum
emissions of powders are also consistent with the bandgaps,
showing coronene (2.44 eV) > 2H-B2N2-C (2.28 eV) > H-
B2N2-C (2.19 eV) > B2N2-C (2.17 eV). This trend contradicts
the observed absorption spectra of single-molecule solution,
indicating the profound effect of intermolecular interaction
(electronic coupling) on bandgaps of solids. The doping of
B─N narrows the bandgap signiﬁcantly with a reduction
of 0.41 eV. With the addition of alkyl chains, the bandgap
gradually increases. The band structures of four single crystals
were also simulated (Figure 5d), showing the same trend as
the above results. Finally, the overlap integrals of HOMO and
hole transfer integrals were calculated to further understand
the electron couplings (Figure 5e). B2N2-C exhibits higher
HOMO–HOMO overlap (0.0153) and transfer integrals
(−124.7 meV) than coronene (0.00491 and −42.6 meV),
signifying the enhanced electron coupling of B2N2-C. 2H-
B2N2-C-rod displays slightly higher HOMO–HOMO overlap
(0.0200) and transfer integral (−151.6 meV) than B2N2-C,
whereas 2H-B2N2-C-plate exhibits tiny values. The stronger
electron coupling of 2H-B2N2-C-rod than B2N2-C is ascribed
to the optimal arrangement of molecules. The above analysis
suggests that B2N2-C with narrowed bandgap of solids and
enhanced electron coupling is expected to be a promising
subunit for future organic electronic materials. Considering
the solution processability, the thin ﬁlm transistors of H-
B2N2-C and 2H-B2N2-C were further fabricated. Only
H-B2N2-C exhibits the charge transport performance with a
hole mobility of 2.8 × 10−4 cm2 V−1 s−1 (Figure S43). The
poor mobility was attributed to the poor morphology caused
by insufﬁcient solubility.

Conclusion
In summary, we synthesized three internally BN-doped
coronenes, B2N2-C, H-B2N2-C, and 2H-B2N-C, for the
ﬁrst time. The internal incorporation of the B─N unit
brings about unique electronic structures and photophysical
properties. Single-crystal analysis shows that B2N2-C retains
the structure of coronene but exhibits stronger π–π stack-
ing, higher electronic coupling, and a narrowed solid-state
bandgap. The B─N dipole–dipole interaction leads to a more
ordered assembly, and each B2N2-coronene exhibits excimer
emission in solution, whereas coronene does not exhibit this
phenomenon. This work not only achieves the synthesis of the
ﬁrst internally BN-doped coronene but also fundamentally
advances our understanding of the regulation of B─N dipole
on intermolecular interactions and assembly. The B─N dipole
provides a new way to regulate the luminescence of molecular
aggregates.

Abstract: We present the ﬁrst synthesis of internally BN-doped coronenes (B2N2-C, H-B2N2-C, and 2H- B2N2-C) with two covalent B─N units embedded on the central axis of coronene. The B─N doping leads to unique electronic structures with distinct charge distribution, conjugation, aromaticity, and photophysical properties. The structures were successfully identiﬁed by the single-crystal X-ray scattering. B2N2-C without sidechains retains the structure of coronene but exhibits stronger π–π stacking, higher electronic coupling, and a narrowed solid-state bandgap. Driven by the B─N dipole–dipole interaction, all B2N2-coronene derivatives exhibit more ordered assembly with excimer emission in solution, which is absent in coronene. Notably, two stable polymorphs emerge in single crystals of 2H-B2N2-C with two hexyl chains: a kinetically stable rod phase and a thermodynamically stable plate phase, where variations in processing conditions direct the formation of different phases.
